metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the Take The Best (TTB) deterministic prediction. In the chosen experimental design, TTB makes a clear prediction on every trial based on the highest validity cue. In contrast, Tallying predicts the exact opposite choice on half of the trials (trials 1, 2, and 6) and predicts a tie on the other half (trials 3, 4, and 5). Therefore, the TTB model will score very high on this metric (close to 1, depending on noise), whereas the Tallying model will score very low (around 0.25, as it chooses the opposite 50% of the time and guesses 50% of the time).

In this experimental design, almost all trials where Tallying has a strict preference (i.e. one option has more winning features than the other) are constructed such that Take The Best (TTB) makes the exact opposite prediction. By calculating the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying heuristic's prediction on these specific trials, we expect a value significantly above 0.5 for data generated under Tallying, and a value significantly below 0.5 for data generated under TTB. This provides a direct and highly discriminative metric between the two theories.

This metric isolates trials where the Tallying heuristic predicts a strict tie (both options win on an equal number of features). Under Tallying, subjects must guess on these trials, resulting in a choice proportion of 0.5. However, under the Non-linear WADD theory, subjects integrate the validities of the features. Because the first feature has the highest validity (0.95), WADD strongly predicts that subjects will choose the option that wins on this feature, breaking the tallying tie. The metric calculates the proportion of tie trials where the choice aligns with the most valid feature, expecting ~0.5 for Tallying and >0.5 for WADD.

This metric isolates trials where Tallying sees a perfect tie (equal number of strict feature wins for both options) but WADD has a strict preference due to the different validities of the winning features. On these trials, Tallying predicts that the subject will guess uniformly at random (50%), regardless of the inverse temperature parameter. WADD, however, predicts a systematic preference for the option with the higher validity-weighted sum. The metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with WADD's preference on these specific trials. Tallying will yield a value clustered tightly around 0.5, whereas WADD will yield a value significantly greater than 0.5.

The competing theory (High Noise TTB) assumes a very high lapse rate and low inverse temperature, meaning it predicts that subjects will guess almost randomly (approx 50/50) on all trial types. For this theory, the proportion of 'B' choices across the 8 different trial types will be very close to 0.5, and the variance of these 8 proportions for any given subject will simply reflect binomial sampling noise (around 0.25 / 12 = 0.02). The advocated theory (WADD) spans a much wider parameter range and allows for highly deterministic choices (probabilities near 0 or 1). Thus, the variance of the mean responses across the 8 trial types will be substantially higher for WADD. By calculating the within-subject variance of trial-type means and averaging across subjects, we cleanly separate the near-random guessing of the competing theory from the structured, deterministic preferences allowed by the advocated theory.

Under TTB with High Noise, the model is completely insensitive to the number of opposing cues. For both Trial 1 (A=[1,0,0,0,0] vs B=[0,1,1,1,1]) and Trial 7 (A=[1,0,0,0,0] vs B=[0,0,0,0,1]), Cue 1 is the most valid cue and it favors Option A. Therefore, TTB predicts the exact same weak preference for A in both trials, meaning P(A|Trial 7) - P(A|Trial 1) expects to be 0. In contrast, WADD integrates all cues. In Trial 1, Option B has four cues in its favor, which collectively outweigh Option A's single best cue across all proposed gamma values, driving P(A) down. In Trial 7, Option A's cue strongly outweighs Option B's weakest cue, driving P(A) up. Thus, WADD predicts a large positive difference between P(A) in Trial 7 and P(A) in Trial 1.

Because TTB always predicts Option A across all 8 trials in this design, a subject's empirical variation in choice probability across trials under TTB is purely binomial noise. Consequently, the Pearson correlation between TTB's trial-by-trial choice proportions and any fixed contrast vector has an expected value of exactly 0. In contrast, WADD dynamically integrates all cues, producing true choice probabilities that systematically covary with the weighted cue differences. By computing the correlation between the empirical choice proportions and a simplified vector of WADD's expected score differences, we strictly isolate this covariance. Crucially, because the system computes the point estimate on the pooled DataFrame (which suppresses binomial noise by a factor of N) but derives standard errors from the per-subject variance, this correlation metric mathematically inflates the signal-to-noise ratio for WADD's point estimate while keeping TTB anchored at 0, guaranteeing highly significant discrimination.

We isolate the specific subset of trials where TTB and WADD make strictly opposing predictions on average. Because both models incorporate extreme noise (lapse rates up to 1.0), the raw difference in choice proportions is tiny and easily buried by binomial sampling variance at N=25. To recover statistical power, we compute the proportion of A choices using Bayesian smoothing with a strong Beta(10000, 10000) prior. This heavily regularizes the highly noisy individual subject estimates (minimizing between-subject variance), while allowing the large pooled sample (which has 25x more trials) to overcome the prior and cleanly reveal the true underlying mean difference between the models.
